title: Rethinking Batch Composition: Promoting feature diversity for Speech Enhancement

paper.title: Rethinking Batch Composition: Promoting feature diversity for Speech Enhancement
paper.abstract: Abstract Speech enhancement systems are commonly trained using randomly sampled mini-batches, which may contain limited diversity in intrinsic acoustic characteristics of the clean speech signals. Motivated by previous findings linking clean speech characteristics to enhancement performance, we propose a feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that divides training examples into quantiles according to a clean-speech characteristic and enforces equal representation within each mini-batch. Experiments across two large-scale English and Spanish speech datasets and a smaller dataset containing neurotypical and pathological speech demonstrate improvements over standard random mini-batch sampling across multiple objective enhancement metrics. Ablation studies demonstrate that the gains are robust across training runs, while their magnitude depends on the acoustic characteristic used for stratification. The proposed strategy requires no modification to the enhancement model or training objective, providing a simple and complementary approach to speech enhancement training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Speech enhancement (SE) aims to improve the quality and intelligibility of speech degraded by noise, reverberation, and other acoustic distortions. A broad range of deep learning-based approaches has been developed for this task, including discriminative and generative approaches. Discriminative approaches learn a mapping from degraded to clean speech through, e.g., spectral mask estimation [ 1 ] or spectral coefficient estimation [ 2 ] , whereas generative approaches formulate SE as a probabilistic generation problem using diffusion [ 3 ] , flow matching [ 4 ] , or Schrödinger Bridge [ 5 ] . Despite their overall strong performance, these approaches can exhibit substantial performance differences across input conditions, with a range of factors, such as e.g., acoustic degradation (noise type, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)) [ 6 ] or characteristics of the target speaker [ 7 ] , contributing to this variability. This challenge has motivated efforts to improve SE robustness and generalization. For example, robustness to different acoustic conditions has been addressed by explicitly accounting for noise type and SNR [ 8 , 9 ] or by using mixture-of-experts architectures in which different model components can specialize to different acoustic conditions [ 10 ] . To achieve consistent performance across speakers, speaker-aware and personalized SE approaches have been proposed that condition enhancement on speaker embeddings or that adapt models to individual speakers [ 7 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Beyond explicitly targeting robustness to acoustic conditions or different speakers, improvements to SE generalization have also been pursued through alternative loss functions [ 14 ] , training targets [ 15 , 16 ] , and model architectures [ 17 , 18 ] , as well as through strategies for improving the quality and scale of training data [ 19 ] . Despite these advances, recent studies have shown that certain speech samples remain challenging for state-of-the-art SE models, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are fixed [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . This suggests that an important source of enhancement difficulty lies in the intrinsic characteristics of the clean speech signal itself. In our previous work [ 22 ] , we demonstrated that clean speech characteristics such as formant structure and loudness can be strongly correlated with SE performance, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are controlled. To the best of our knowledge, this source of variability has never been considered in the design of SE training strategies. Specifically, training data are typically presented to SE models through randomly sampled mini-batches, without explicitly considering the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics within each batch. Although random sampling provides unbiased coverage of the training set over many iterations, individual mini-batches can still differ substantially in their acoustic composition. For speech data with high intrinsic variability, a randomly sampled batch may consequently cover only a limited region of the acoustic feature space, causing individual gradient updates to be dominated by a restricted range of enhancement difficulty. In this work, we propose to explicitly control the distribution of intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch to improve SE training and performance. To this end, we propose a simple plug-and-play feature-stratified sampling strategy. For each training sample, we extract a user-defined clean speech characteristic (such as e.g., the mean formant frequency or the mean loudness) and partition the training data into quantiles based on its value. Each mini-batch is then constructed with an equal number of samples from each quantile. Importantly, the selected characteristic is used solely to determine the composition of the mini-batch and is not provided as an input to the SE model. We evaluate the proposed strategy on discriminative and generative SE approaches across two languages, i.e., English and Spanish, and across two speaker populations, i.e., neuortypical and pathological. Across these various datasets, we observe consistent improvements in multiple objective SE metrics when the proposed feature-stratified sampling strategy is used for training. The main contributions of this work are: 1. We introduce feature-stratified batch sampling for SE, a simple plug-and-play training strategy that explicitly promotes diversity in intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch. 2. We demonstrate consistent performance improvements across two SE paradigms, two languages, and two speaker groups, using four objective SE metrics. 3. We show that the improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch sampling, and that their magnitude depends on the clean speech characteristic used for stratification. In particular, characteristics that are strongly associated with SE performance provide greater benefits, suggesting that stratification is most effective when it promotes diversity along acoustic dimensions related to enhancement difficulty.

sections.text: The noisy microphone signal y ⁡ ( t ) y(t) at time t t is given by the sum of the clean speech signal s ⁡ ( t ) s(t) and the noise signal n ⁡ ( t ) n(t) , i.e., y ⁡ ( t ) = s ⁡ ( t ) + n ⁡ ( t ) . y(t)=s(t)+n(t). (1) In the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain, ( 1 ) is given by Y ⁡ ( f , k ) = S ⁡ ( f , k ) + N ⁡ ( f , k ) , \displaystyle Y(f,k)=S(f,k)+N(f,k), (2) where Y ⁡ ( f , k ) Y(f,k) , S ⁡ ( f , k ) S(f,k) , and N ⁡ ( f , k ) N(f,k) denote the complex-valued STFT coefficients of the noisy, clean speech, and noise signals, respectively, and f f and k k denote the frequency bin and time frame indices. The objective of SE is to recover the clean speech signal from its noisy observation. Depending on the modeling paradigm, this objective can be formulated as a direct regression problem or as a generative mapping problem between noisy and clean speech. In this work, we consider representative state-of-the-art models from both paradigms, which are briefly described below. Their implementation and training configurations are detailed in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 2.1 Speech enhancement models
sections.text: Complex-valued spectrogram-based regression (CR): CR follows a discriminative regression formulation in which a deep neural network predicts the real and imaginary components of the clean speech STFT from the corresponding noisy STFT [ 23 ] . The predicted complex-valued spectrum is transformed back to the time domain, and the model is optimized using the mean square error between the reconstructed signal s ^ ​ ( t ) \hat{s}(t) and the clean signal s ⁡ ( t ) s(t) . Schrödinger Bridge-based model (SB): In contrast to direct regression, SB formulates SE as a generative transport problem learning a stochastic path between the noisy observation and the corresponding clean speech representation [ 24 , 5 ] . Unlike conventional diffusion-based approaches which progressively perturb clean speech toward a predefined noise distribution [ 3 ] , SB learns this path directly from the paired noisy and clean representations. The model is trained with a weighted data-prediction objective defined in both the time and STFT domains. Further details of the SB formulation are provided in [ 5 ] .

sections.heading: 2.2 Training procedure
sections.text: State-of-the-art SE models are conventionally trained using mini-batches formed by randomly sampling training examples. We consider a training set 𝒟 \mathcal{D} consisting of N N pairs of clean-noisy examples, i.e., 𝒟 = { ( s i , y i ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\{(s_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where s i s_{i} denotes the i i -th clean signal and y i y_{i} denotes the corresponding noisy observation. Standard SE training constructs a mini-batch by randomly sampling B B examples from 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . We use this random sampling strategy as the baseline for training the CR and SB models and compare it against the proposed stratified sampling strategy described in Section 3 .

sections.heading: 3 Proposed method
sections.text: Conventional random sampling treats all training examples equally, irrespective of their intrinsic speech characteristics. Our previous analysis showed that intrinsic properties of clean speech are correlated with enhancement gains [ 22 ] , suggesting that the distribution of such characteristics in the training data may influence how effectively an SE model learns across different types of speech. This motivates us to investigate whether explicitly controlling the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics during training can improve model generalization. We therefore propose a stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that balances the representation of a (user-defined) clean speech characteristic across training batches. The approach is independent of the specific characteristic used for stratification and modifies only how training examples are sampled.

sections.heading: 3.1 Speech characteristics
sections.text: We extract intrinsic speech characteristics from the clean training utterances using the openSMILE toolkit [ 25 ] . Let f ⁡ ( s i ) f(s_{i}) denote the value of a selected characteristic for the clean signal s i s_{i} . The characteristic is computed once for each training utterance and is used solely to determine its sampling group, i.e., it is not provided as an input to the enhancement model. In our experiments, we consider the mean third formant frequency F 3 F_{3} (cf. Section 5.1 ) and the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} (cf. Section 5.2 ) as speech characteristics for stratification.

sections.heading: 3.2 Stratified mini-batch sampling
sections.text: For a given batch size B B , we propose to choose the number of quantiles J J such that B B is divisible by J J . The empirical distribution of the selected characteristic f ⁡ ( s i ) f(s_{i}) over the training set is divided into J J quantiles, denoted by Q 1 Q_{1} , … \ldots , Q J Q_{J} . Each training example is assigned to exactly one quantile according to its characteristic value. Each mini-batch is constructed by randomly sampling B / J B/J utterances from each quantile. Sampling is performed without replacement within an epoch, while the examples are reshuffled between epochs. Thus, each mini-batch contains an equal representation of utterances spanning the range of the selected clean speech characteristic, rather than reflecting a potentially imbalanced distribution. The quantile boundaries are computed once using the training set and remain fixed throughout training. The same sampling procedure can be applied independently to any SE model, allowing the effect of stratified sampling to be evaluated without modifying the underlying SE architectures, training objectives, or optimization procedures. The proposed strategy can be implemented using a custom sampler in standard deep learning data loading frameworks.

sections.heading: 4.1 Datasets
sections.text: Clean speech signals. To assess the generalizability of our findings across languages, we use two clean speech datasets, i.e., the English Wall Street Journal (WSJ0) dataset [ 26 ] and the Crowdsourced Latin American Spanish (CROWD) dataset [ 27 ] . WSJ0 is a commonly used benchmark for SE [ 3 , 5 ] , containing 28.6 28.6 hours of speech from 120 120 speakers. We use the standard WSJ0 split, with 101 101 , 10 10 , and 8 8 speakers assigned to the train, validation, and test sets, respectively. Since the CROWD dataset is larger, we select subsets of it with a comparable duration and the same number of speakers as the different WSJ0 splits. To assess the impact of the proposed batch sampling strategy across neurotypical and pathological speaker groups, we additionally use the PC-GITA dataset [ 28 ] . PC-GITA contains 2.8 2.8 hours of speech from 50 50 individuals with Parkinson’s disease and 50 50 neurotypical controls. Each speaker produces 12 12 utterances, comprising 10 10 sentences, one read text, and one monologue. Given the limited amount of available speech, we use speaker-independent 10 10 -fold cross-validation for the PC-GITA dataset [ 13 , 22 ] . In each fold, 80 % 80\% , 10 % 10\% , and 10 % 10\% of the speakers are assigned to the training, validation, and test sets, respectively. For each dataset, all recordings are downsampled to 16 16 kHz and the SE models are trained and evaluated independently using only the corresponding training, validation, and test data. Noisy mixtures. Noisy mixtures are constructed using four environmental noise categories from CHiME3 [ 29 ] , i.e., bus, cafe, pedestrian area, and street. Noise recordings are first downsampled to 16 16 kHz before mixture generation. A random segment of a randomly selected noise category is added to a clean speech signal. The mixture SNR is sampled uniformly from − 6 -6 dB to 14 14 dB. This procedure follows the noise-mixing protocol commonly adopted in previous SE studies [ 23 , 5 ] .

sections.heading: 4.2 Model architectures and training
sections.text: Following [ 23 ] , signals are transformed to the STFT domain using a window size of 510 510 samples, a hop length of 128 128 samples, and a Hann window. The STFT coefficients are then compressed using α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 and β = 0.33 \beta=0.33 as in [ 5 ] . Both the CR and SB models use the NCSN++M U-Net architecture, a lighter configuration of NCSN++ [ 30 , 23 ] . The CR model removes the noise-conditioning layers, resulting in 22.1 22.1 million trainable parameters, whereas the SB model retains these layers, resulting in 25.2 25.2 million trainable parameters. In addition, SB uses exponential moving average with a decay rate of 0.999 0.999 [ 5 ] , a variance-exploding noise schedule with σ min = 0.7 \sigma_{\min}=0.7 and σ max = 1.82 \sigma_{\max}=1.82 , and 50 50 -step SDE sampling. Training is performed using the Adam optimizer, a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and a maximum of 1000 1000 epochs. Training stops if the validation loss does not decrease for 20 20 consecutive epochs. For the WSJ0 and CROWD dataset, models are trained on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. For the PC-GITA dataset, models are trained on an RTX 3090 GPU.

sections.heading: 4.3 Evaluation
sections.text: SE performance is evaluated using four established objective metrics, i.e., extended short-time objective intelligibility (ESTOI) [ 31 ] , wideband perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) [ 32 ] , frequency-weighted segmental signal-to-noise ratio (fwSSNR) [ 33 ] , and scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) [ 34 ] . The clean speech signal is used as the reference signal for all metrics. sections.heading: 5 Experimental Results
sections.text: This section evaluates the effectiveness of the proposed stratified mini-batch sampling strategy and examines the factors that influence its performance and robustness. We first compare the proposed strategy with standard random mini-batch sampling across the considered SE models and speech datasets (Section 5.1 ). For these main experiments, the mean value of F 3 F_{3} is used as the acoustic characteristic for stratification, motivated by its strong correlation with SE performance observed in our previous work [ 22 ] . We then conduct two ablation studies. First, we investigate whether the choice of acoustic characteristic affects the benefit of stratification by comparing mean F 3 F_{3} with the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} , which showed little or no correlation with SE performance in our previous work (Section 5.2 ). Second, we assess whether the observed improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch composition by comparing random and stratified sampling across multiple training runs (Section 5.3 ).

Models are separately trained and tested on the English WSJ0, Spanish CROWD, and Spanish PC-GITA datasets. For PC-GITA, test performance is reported separately for neurotypical and pathological speakers. For the WSJ0 dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, with the largest gains observed for the CR model, particularly in E-STOI and fwSSNR. Improvements for the SB model are more modest across all metrics. For the CROWD dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, but the improvements are more pronounced for the SB model, particularly for PESQ, fwSSNR, and SI-SDR. For the PC-GITA dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of the CR model for both neurotypical and pathological speakers, with the largest gains observed in E-STOI and fwSSNR. In contrast, the SB model achieves performance comparable to random sampling, with only minor differences between the two strategies. The consistent gains of the CR model across both speaker groups indicate that the proposed sampling strategy also benefits pathological speech. Overall, stratified mini-batch sampling maintains or improves performance across both SE models, all three datasets, and both neurotypical and pathological speaker populations, with the magnitude of the gains depending on the dataset, model architecture, and evaluation metric. The strategy requires virtually no additional computational cost and leaves the enhancement model, training objective, data, and optimization procedure unchanged, modifying only how training examples are selected to form mini-batches. Therefore, it provides a simple and complementary means of improving SE training and performance without additional model complexity.

sections.heading: 5.2 Effect of the acoustic characteristic used for stratification
sections.text: The mean F 3 F_{3} was selected as the stratification feature for the results in Section 5.1 based on its strong correlation with SE performance reported in our previous work [ 22 ] . To examine whether the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy depends on this correlation, we additionally consider the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} as the stratification feature, which exhibits little or no correlation with SE performance [ 22 ] . As an exemplary setting for this ablation study, we consider the CR model trained and evaluated on the English WSJ0 dataset. Table 2 compares the performance of the CR model on WSJ0 when using mean F 3 F_{3} and the standard deviation of f 0 f_{0} for stratification. The mean F 3 F_{3} results are repeated from Section 5.1 to facilitate a direct comparison. It can be observed that stratification based on mean F 3 F_{3} yields considerable improvements over the standard deviation of f 0 f_{0} for E-STOI and fwSSNR, whereas PESQ and SI-SDR remain comparable. This suggests that the effectiveness of stratification is not determined simply by introducing greater acoustic diversity within a mini-batch. Instead, the diversity appears to be more beneficial when it is introduced along a dimension that reflects differences in enhancement difficulty.

sections.heading: 5.3 Robustness to stochastic mini-batch sampling
sections.text: The results in Section 5.1 are obtained from a single training run. Since stochastic mini-batch sampling can lead to different mini-batch compositions across training runs, we additionally examine whether the observed performance differences between random and stratified sampling are robust to such variations. To this end, we train the CR model on the English WSJ0 dataset using three independent training runs, with the same random seeds applied to both sampling strategies. For stratified sampling, the mean F 3 F_{3} is used as the stratification feature. Table 3 reports the resulting performance across the three runs. The results show that stratified sampling consistently outperforms random sampling across all four metrics. The relatively small standard deviations across runs indicate that these improvements are consistent across different random seeds, suggesting that the benefit of stratified sampling is robust to stochastic variation in mini-batch composition.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Outlook
sections.text: In this paper, we proposed a simple feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy for training SE models. The strategy divides the training data according to a clean-speech characteristic strongly correlated with SE performance, i.e., the mean F 3 F_{3} , and enforces equal representation of its quantiles within each mini-batch. The proposed strategy improves SE performance across multiple models, datasets, and evaluation metrics, although the magnitude of the gains varies across experimental conditions. The proposed method requires no modification to the enhancement architecture, loss function, or training procedure, and can be readily incorporated into existing training pipelines. Future work will explore joint diversification based on multiple acoustic characteristics, curriculum learning strategies, effects of different batch sizes and number of quantiles, as well as subjective evaluation of the resulting enhanced speech.

sections.heading: 7 Compliance with Ethical Standards
sections.text: This research study was conducted retrospectively using human subject data made available in [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] . Ethical approval was not required as confirmed by the license attached with the data.

Abstract Speech enhancement systems are commonly trained using randomly sampled mini-batches, which may contain limited diversity in intrinsic acoustic characteristics of the clean speech signals. Motivated by previous findings linking clean speech characteristics to enhancement performance, we propose a feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that divides training examples into quantiles according to a clean-speech characteristic and enforces equal representation within each mini-batch. Experiments across two large-scale English and Spanish speech datasets and a smaller dataset containing neurotypical and pathological speech demonstrate improvements over standard random mini-batch sampling across multiple objective enhancement metrics. Ablation studies demonstrate that the gains are robust across training runs, while their magnitude depends on the acoustic characteristic used for stratification. The proposed strategy requires no modification to the enhancement model or training objective, providing a simple and complementary approach to speech enhancement training. Index Terms: speech enhancement, mini-batch composition, intrinsic acoustic feature † † address: 1 Idiap Research Institute, Switzerland 2 École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Switzerland 1 Introduction Speech enhancement (SE) aims to improve the quality and intelligibility of speech degraded by noise, reverberation, and other acoustic distortions. A broad range of deep learning-based approaches has been developed for this task, including discriminative and generative approaches. Discriminative approaches learn a mapping from degraded to clean speech through, e.g., spectral mask estimation [ 1 ] or spectral coefficient estimation [ 2 ] , whereas generative approaches formulate SE as a probabilistic generation problem using diffusion [ 3 ] , flow matching [ 4 ] , or Schrödinger Bridge [ 5 ] . Despite their overall strong performance, these approaches can exhibit substantial performance differences across input conditions, with a range of factors, such as e.g., acoustic degradation (noise type, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)) [ 6 ] or characteristics of the target speaker [ 7 ] , contributing to this variability. This challenge has motivated efforts to improve SE robustness and generalization. For example, robustness to different acoustic conditions has been addressed by explicitly accounting for noise type and SNR [ 8 , 9 ] or by using mixture-of-experts architectures in which different model components can specialize to different acoustic conditions [ 10 ] . To achieve consistent performance across speakers, speaker-aware and personalized SE approaches have been proposed that condition enhancement on speaker embeddings or that adapt models to individual speakers [ 7 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Beyond explicitly targeting robustness to acoustic conditions or different speakers, improvements to SE generalization have also been pursued through alternative loss functions [ 14 ] , training targets [ 15 , 16 ] , and model architectures [ 17 , 18 ] , as well as through strategies for improving the quality and scale of training data [ 19 ] . Despite these advances, recent studies have shown that certain speech samples remain challenging for state-of-the-art SE models, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are fixed [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . This suggests that an important source of enhancement difficulty lies in the intrinsic characteristics of the clean speech signal itself. In our previous work [ 22 ] , we demonstrated that clean speech characteristics such as formant structure and loudness can be strongly correlated with SE performance, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are controlled. To the best of our knowledge, this source of variability has never been considered in the design of SE training strategies. Specifically, training data are typically presented to SE models through randomly sampled mini-batches, without explicitly considering the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics within each batch. Although random sampling provides unbiased coverage of the training set over many iterations, individual mini-batches can still differ substantially in their acoustic composition. For speech data with high intrinsic variability, a randomly sampled batch may consequently cover only a limited region of the acoustic feature space, causing individual gradient updates to be dominated by a restricted range of enhancement difficulty. In this work, we propose to explicitly control the distribution of intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch to improve SE training and performance. To this end, we propose a simple plug-and-play feature-stratified sampling strategy. For each training sample, we extract a user-defined clean speech characteristic (such as e.g., the mean formant frequency or the mean loudness) and partition the training data into quantiles based on its value. Each mini-batch is then constructed with an equal number of samples from each quantile. Importantly, the selected characteristic is used solely to determine the composition of the mini-batch and is not provided as an input to the SE model. We evaluate the proposed strategy on discriminative and generative SE approaches across two languages, i.e., English and Spanish, and across two speaker populations, i.e., neuortypical and pathological. Across these various datasets, we observe consistent improvements in multiple objective SE metrics when the proposed feature-stratified sampling strategy is used for training. The main contributions of this work are: 1. We introduce feature-stratified batch sampling for SE, a simple plug-and-play training strategy that explicitly promotes diversity in intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch. 2. We demonstrate consistent performance improvements across two SE paradigms, two languages, and two speaker groups, using four objective SE metrics. 3. We show that the improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch sampling, and that their magnitude depends on the clean speech characteristic used for stratification. In particular, characteristics that are strongly associated with SE performance provide greater benefits, suggesting that stratification is most effective when it promotes diversity along acoustic dimensions related to enhancement difficulty. 2 Speech Enhancement The noisy microphone signal y ⁡ ( t ) y(t) at time t t is given by the sum of the clean speech signal s ⁡ ( t ) s(t) and the noise signal n ⁡ ( t ) n(t) , i.e., y ⁡ ( t ) = s ⁡ ( t ) + n ⁡ ( t ) . y(t)=s(t)+n(t). (1) In the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain, ( 1 ) is given by Y ⁡ ( f , k ) = S ⁡ ( f , k ) + N ⁡ ( f , k ) , \displaystyle Y(f,k)=S(f,k)+N(f,k), (2) where Y ⁡ ( f , k ) Y(f,k) , S ⁡ ( f , k ) S(f,k) , and N ⁡ ( f , k ) N(f,k) denote the complex-valued STFT coefficients of the noisy, clean speech, and noise signals, respectively, and f f and k k denote the frequency bin and time frame indices. The objective of SE is to recover the clean speech signal from its noisy observation. Depending on the modeling paradigm, this objective can be formulated as a direct regression problem or as a generative mapping problem between noisy and clean speech. In this work, we consider representative state-of-the-art models from both paradigms, which are briefly described below. Their implementation and training configurations are detailed in Section 4 . 2.1 Speech enhancement models Complex-valued spectrogram-based regression (CR): CR follows a discriminative regression formulation in which a deep neural network predicts the real and imaginary components of the clean speech STFT from the corresponding noisy STFT [ 23 ] . The predicted complex-valued spectrum is transformed back to the time domain, and the model is optimized using the mean square error between the reconstructed signal s ^ ​ ( t ) \hat{s}(t) and the clean signal s ⁡ ( t ) s(t) . Schrödinger Bridge-based model (SB): In contrast to direct regression, SB formulates SE as a generative transport problem learning a stochastic path between the noisy observation and the corresponding clean speech representation [ 24 , 5 ] . Unlike conventional diffusion-based approaches which progressively perturb clean speech toward a predefined noise distribution [ 3 ] , SB learns this path directly from the paired noisy and clean representations. The model is trained with a weighted data-prediction objective defined in both the time and STFT domains. Further details of the SB formulation are provided in [ 5 ] . 2.2 Training procedure State-of-the-art SE models are conventionally trained using mini-batches formed by randomly sampling training examples. We consider a training set 𝒟 \mathcal{D} consisting of N N pairs of clean-noisy examples, i.e., 𝒟 = { ( s i , y i ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\{(s_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where s i s_{i} denotes the i i -th clean signal and y i y_{i} denotes the corresponding noisy observation. Standard SE training constructs a mini-batch by randomly sampling B B examples from 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . We use this random sampling strategy as the baseline for training the CR and SB models and compare it against the proposed stratified sampling strategy described in Section 3 . 3 Proposed method Conventional random sampling treats all training examples equally, irrespective of their intrinsic speech characteristics. Our previous analysis showed that intrinsic properties of clean speech are correlated with enhancement gains [ 22 ] , suggesting that the distribution of such characteristics in the training data may influence how effectively an SE model learns across different types of speech. This motivates us to investigate whether explicitly controlling the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics during training can improve model generalization. We therefore propose a stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that balances the representation of a (user-defined) clean speech characteristic across training batches. The approach is independent of the specific characteristic used for stratification and modifies only how training examples are sampled. 3.1 Speech characteristics We extract intrinsic speech characteristics from the clean training utterances using the openSMILE toolkit [ 25 ] . Let f ⁡ ( s i ) f(s_{i}) denote the value of a selected characteristic for the clean signal s i s_{i} . The characteristic is computed once for each training utterance and is used solely to determine its sampling group, i.e., it is not provided as an input to the enhancement model. In our experiments, we consider the mean third formant frequency F 3 F_{3} (cf. Section 5.1 ) and the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} (cf. Section 5.2 ) as speech characteristics for stratification. 3.2 Stratified mini-batch sampling For a given batch size B B , we propose to choose the number of quantiles J J such that B B is divisible by J J . The empirical distribution of the selected characteristic f ⁡ ( s i ) f(s_{i}) over the training set is divided into J J quantiles, denoted by Q 1 Q_{1} , … \ldots , Q J Q_{J} . Each training example is assigned to exactly one quantile according to its characteristic value. Each mini-batch is constructed by randomly sampling B / J B/J utterances from each quantile. Sampling is performed without replacement within an epoch, while the examples are reshuffled between epochs. Thus, each mini-batch contains an equal representation of utterances spanning the range of the selected clean speech characteristic, rather than reflecting a potentially imbalanced distribution. The quantile boundaries are computed once using the training set and remain fixed throughout training. The same sampling procedure can be applied independently to any SE model, allowing the effect of stratified sampling to be evaluated without modifying the underlying SE architectures, training objectives, or optimization procedures. The proposed strategy can be implemented using a custom sampler in standard deep learning data loading frameworks. 4 Experimental settings 4.1 Datasets Clean speech signals. To assess the generalizability of our findings across languages, we use two clean speech datasets, i.e., the English Wall Street Journal (WSJ0) dataset [ 26 ] and the Crowdsourced Latin American Spanish (CROWD) dataset [ 27 ] . WSJ0 is a commonly used benchmark for SE [ 3 , 5 ] , containing 28.6 28.6 hours of speech from 120 120 speakers. We use the standard WSJ0 split, with 101 101 , 10 10 , and 8 8 speakers assigned to the train, validation, and test sets, respectively. Since the CROWD dataset is larger, we select subsets of it with a comparable duration and the same number of speakers as the different WSJ0 splits. To assess the impact of the proposed batch sampling strategy across neurotypical and pathological speaker groups, we additionally use the PC-GITA dataset [ 28 ] . PC-GITA contains 2.8 2.8 hours of speech from 50 50 individuals with Parkinson’s disease and 50 50 neurotypical controls. Each speaker produces 12 12 utterances, comprising 10 10 sentences, one read text, and one monologue. Given the limited amount of available speech, we use speaker-independent 10 10 -fold cross-validation for the PC-GITA dataset [ 13 , 22 ] . In each fold, 80 % 80\% , 10 % 10\% , and 10 % 10\% of the speakers are assigned to the training, validation, and test sets, respectively. For each dataset, all recordings are downsampled to 16 16 kHz and the SE models are trained and evaluated independently using only the corresponding training, validation, and test data. Noisy mixtures. Noisy mixtures are constructed using four environmental noise categories from CHiME3 [ 29 ] , i.e., bus, cafe, pedestrian area, and street. Noise recordings are first downsampled to 16 16 kHz before mixture generation. A random segment of a randomly selected noise category is added to a clean speech signal. The mixture SNR is sampled uniformly from − 6 -6 dB to 14 14 dB. This procedure follows the noise-mixing protocol commonly adopted in previous SE studies [ 23 , 5 ] . 4.2 Model architectures and training Following [ 23 ] , signals are transformed to the STFT domain using a window size of 510 510 samples, a hop length of 128 128 samples, and a Hann window. The STFT coefficients are then compressed using α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 and β = 0.33 \beta=0.33 as in [ 5 ] . Both the CR and SB models use the NCSN++M U-Net architecture, a lighter configuration of NCSN++ [ 30 , 23 ] . The CR model removes the noise-conditioning layers, resulting in 22.1 22.1 million trainable parameters, whereas the SB model retains these layers, resulting in 25.2 25.2 million trainable parameters. In addition, SB uses exponential moving average with a decay rate of 0.999 0.999 [ 5 ] , a variance-exploding noise schedule with σ min = 0.7 \sigma_{\min}=0.7 and σ max = 1.82 \sigma_{\max}=1.82 , and 50 50 -step SDE sampling. Training is performed using the Adam optimizer, a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and a maximum of 1000 1000 epochs. Training stops if the validation loss does not decrease for 20 20 consecutive epochs. For the WSJ0 and CROWD dataset, models are trained on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. For the PC-GITA dataset, models are trained on an RTX 3090 GPU. 4.3 Evaluation SE performance is evaluated using four established objective metrics, i.e., extended short-time objective intelligibility (ESTOI) [ 31 ] , wideband perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) [ 32 ] , frequency-weighted segmental signal-to-noise ratio (fwSSNR) [ 33 ] , and scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) [ 34 ] . The clean speech signal is used as the reference signal for all metrics. To facilitate comparisons across datasets, we report the improvement in these objective metrics, i.e., Δ \Delta ESTOI, Δ \Delta PESQ, Δ \Delta fwSSNR, and Δ \Delta SI-SDR, relative to the noisy mixture. influence its performance and robustness. We first compare the proposed strategy with standard random mini-batch sampling across the considered SE models and speech datasets (Section 5.1 ). For these main experiments, the mean value of F 3 F_{3} is used as the acoustic characteristic for stratification, motivated by its strong correlation with SE performance observed in our previous work [ 22 ] . We then conduct two ablation studies. First, we investigate whether the choice of acoustic characteristic affects the benefit of stratification by comparing mean F 3 F_{3} with the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} , which showed little or no correlation with SE performance in our previous work (Section 5.2 ). Second, we assess whether the observed improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch composition by comparing random and stratified sampling across multiple training runs (Section 5.3 ). 5.1 SE performance using standard and stratified mini-batch sampling Table 2: Performance [mean ± \pm 95 % 95\% confidence interval] of the CR model trained with stratified mini-batch sampling using the mean F 3 F_{3} and the standard deviation of f 0 f_{0} as stratification features on the English WSJ0 dataset. Models are separately trained and tested on the English WSJ0, Spanish CROWD, and Spanish PC-GITA datasets. For PC-GITA, test performance is reported separately for neurotypical and pathological speakers. For the WSJ0 dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, with the largest gains observed for the CR model, particularly in E-STOI and fwSSNR. Improvements for the SB model are more modest across all metrics. For the CROWD dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, but the improvements are more pronounced for the SB model, particularly for PESQ, fwSSNR, and SI-SDR. For the PC-GITA dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of the CR model for both neurotypical and pathological speakers, with the largest gains observed in E-STOI and fwSSNR. In contrast, the SB model achieves performance comparable to random sampling, with only minor differences between the two strategies. The consistent gains of the CR model across both speaker groups indicate that the proposed sampling strategy also benefits pathological speech. Overall, stratified mini-batch sampling maintains or improves performance across both SE models, all three datasets, and both neurotypical and pathological speaker populations, with the magnitude of the gains depending on the dataset, model architecture, and evaluation metric. The strategy requires virtually no additional computational cost and leaves the enhancement model, training objective, data, and optimization procedure unchanged, modifying only how training examples are selected to form mini-batches. Therefore, it provides a simple and complementary means of improving SE training and performance without additional model complexity. 5.2 Effect of the acoustic characteristic used for stratification The mean F 3 F_{3} was selected as the stratification feature for the results in Section 5.1 based on its strong correlation with SE performance reported in our previous work [ 22 ] . To examine whether the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy depends on this correlation, we additionally consider the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f 0 f_{0} as the stratification feature, which exhibits little or no correlation with SE performance [ 22 ] . As an exemplary setting for this ablation study, we consider the CR model trained and evaluated on the English WSJ0 dataset. Table 2 compares the performance of the CR model on WSJ0 when using mean F 3 F_{3} and the standard deviation of f 0 f_{0} for stratification. The mean F 3 F_{3} results are repeated from Section 5.1 to facilitate a direct comparison. It can be observed that stratification based on mean F 3 F_{3} yields considerable improvements over the standard deviation of f 0 f_{0} for E-STOI and fwSSNR, whereas PESQ and SI-SDR remain comparable. This suggests that the effectiveness of stratification is not determined simply by introducing greater acoustic diversity within a mini-batch. Instead, the diversity appears to be more beneficial when it is introduced along a dimension that reflects differences in enhancement difficulty. 5.3 Robustness to stochastic mini-batch sampling The results in Section 5.1 are obtained from a single training run. Since stochastic mini-batch sampling can lead to different mini-batch compositions across training runs, we additionally examine whether the observed performance differences between random and stratified sampling are robust to such variations. To this end, we train the CR model on the English WSJ0 dataset using three independent training runs, with the same random seeds applied to both sampling strategies. For stratified sampling, the mean F 3 F_{3} is used as the stratification feature. Table 3 reports the resulting performance across the three runs. The results show that stratified sampling consistently outperforms random sampling across all four metrics. The relatively small standard deviations across runs indicate that these improvements are consistent across different random seeds, suggesting that the benefit of stratified sampling is robust to stochastic variation in mini-batch composition. 6 Conclusion and Outlook In this paper, we proposed a simple feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy for training SE models. The strategy divides the training data according to a clean-speech characteristic strongly correlated with SE performance, i.e., the mean F 3 F_{3} , and enforces equal representation of its quantiles within each mini-batch. The proposed strategy improves SE performance across multiple models, datasets, and evaluation metrics, although the magnitude of the gains varies across experimental conditions. The proposed method requires no modification to the enhancement architecture, loss function, or training procedure, and can be readily incorporated into existing training pipelines. Future work will explore joint diversification based on multiple acoustic characteristics, curriculum learning strategies, effects of different batch sizes and number of quantiles, as well as subjective evaluation of the resulting enhanced speech. 7 Compliance with Ethical Standards This research study was conducted retrospectively using human subject data made available in [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] .
